sourceDate.text: 方華合公司設線九龍也
雲南猛喇游匪魏名高之滋事

translationRepairs: When Imperial Commissioner Zeng Jizi sent a telegram from Russia to Shanghai, it took only one day.
When Imperial Commissioner Zeng Jize sent a telegram from Russia to Shanghai, it took only one day.
曾紀澤 is Zeng Jize (Zeng Jize, 1839–1890); Jizi is an incorrect reading of 澤 and should not appear in the idiomatic text.
When the imperial envoy Zeng Jizi telegraphed from Russia to Shanghai, it required only one day.
When the imperial envoy Zeng Jize telegraphed from Russia to Shanghai, it required only one day.
The literal field contains the same mistaken reading of 曾紀澤; Zeng Jize is the correct personal name.
The British minister Granville also invoked precedent to request submarine cables from Shanghai to Ningbo, Wenzhou, Fuzhou, Xiamen, and Shantou.
The British minister Grosvenor also invoked precedent to request submarine cables from Shanghai to Ningbo, Wenzhou, Fuzhou, Xiamen, and Shantou.
格維納 is Thomas George Grosvenor, who served as Britain's chargé d'affaires in China in 1882–1883. Granville was the British foreign secretary, not the British representative described here.
The British minister Granville also cited precedent in requesting additional submarine cables from Shanghai to Ningbo, Wenzhou, Fuzhou, Xiamen, and Shantou.
The British minister Grosvenor also cited precedent in requesting additional submarine cables from Shanghai to Ningbo, Wenzhou, Fuzhou, Xiamen, and Shantou.
The literal field makes the same identification error. Contemporary diplomatic records identify Grosvenor as the British chargé d'affaires in this period.

In 1883, Wade revived the proposal, substituting submarine cables for land lines running from Guangzhou through Fujian and Zhejiang to Shanghai. After months of negotiation, the request was finally approved.

In the ninth year [of Tongzhi, 1870], Wade revived the proposal, substituting submarine cables for land lines running from Guangzhou through Fujian and Zhejiang to Shanghai. After months of negotiation, the request was finally approved.

先是同治間 explicitly opens a Tongzhi-era flashback, so the following 九年 is Tongzhi 9 (1870). Reading it as Guangxu 9 breaks the paragraph's chronology and places Wade's renewed proposal thirteen years too late.
Zuo Zongtang, Governor-General of Jiangsu, built Yangtze lines to Wuhan; Zhang Shusheng, Governor-General of Guangdong, built Guangxi lines to Longzhou.
Zuo Zongtang, Governor-General of Liangjiang, built Yangtze lines to Wuhan; Zhang Shusheng, Governor-General of Guangdong, built Guangxi lines to Longzhou.
江督 is the conventional abbreviation for the Governor-General of Liangjiang. Calling Zuo Zongtang Governor-General of Jiangsu incorrectly narrows the jurisdiction and invents a title not used here.

As the French crisis loomed, Envoy Zeng Jizi requested extending telegraph lines into the capital region, arguing this would bolster prestige to preserve peace and enable rapid coordination in wartime.

As the French crisis loomed, Envoy Zeng Jize requested extending telegraph lines into the capital region, arguing this would bolster prestige to preserve peace and enable rapid coordination in wartime.
曾紀澤 again names Zeng Jize; the correction is required in every occurrence rather than preserving Jizi as a false alias.
Both the Zongli Yamen and Zeng Jizi now agree that extending lines into the capital region is sound policy. We propose building first to Tongzhou, then gradually extending to Beijing."
Both the Zongli Yamen and Zeng Jize now agree that extending lines into the capital region is sound policy. We propose building first to Tongzhou, then gradually extending to Beijing."
The later reference is the same Zeng Jize and must use the corrected romanization consistently.
candidateDispositions: Component of an office recorded in this unit, not a person name.
